title: GERD: Diagnose the Typical Syndrome, Escalate Alarm Features
bottomLine: Typical heartburn/regurgitation without alarm features can often be managed clinically with lifestyle measures and an appropriately dosed acid-suppression trial. Dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting, atypical refractory symptoms or high-risk context changes the pathway toward endoscopy or another diagnosis.
recognize: Burning retrosternal discomfort, acid regurgitation and symptoms after meals/lying down are typical.
Chronic cough, laryngeal symptoms or chest pain can coexist but should not automatically be attributed to reflux without evaluating competing causes.
differentiate: ACS and other cardiac disease must be considered in appropriate chest-pain presentations.
Peptic ulcer disease, eosinophilic esophagitis, motility disorders and functional heartburn can mimic refractory GERD.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding, weight change, vomiting, medications, alcohol/tobacco, pregnancy, obesity and prior response to therapy.
workup: No routine imaging or endoscopy is required for uncomplicated typical GERD responding to therapy.
Use endoscopy for alarm features, significant refractory disease or Barrett/structural questions; ambulatory reflux testing is useful when diagnosis remains uncertain despite appropriate evaluation.
management: Use weight/meal timing/trigger modification when relevant without prescribing unnecessary restrictive diets.
Use a PPI when indicated, timed correctly and at the lowest regimen that maintains control after healing/assessment; step-down or intermittent strategies are appropriate for selected patients.
Refer refractory/alarm/complicated disease for GI evaluation.
medicationSafety: Long-term PPI use should have an ongoing indication rather than being continued automatically; avoid abrupt fear-based discontinuation when a clear indication persists.
Review interactions and pregnancy-specific medication choices when relevant.
redFlags: Chest pain concerning for cardiac disease
counselling: Teach correct PPI timing and which symptoms warrant endoscopic/urgent reassessment.
followUp: Confirm response and indication; persistent symptoms despite correct therapy require diagnostic reconsideration rather than indefinite dose escalation.
examTrap: Escalating acid suppression repeatedly for progressive dysphagia instead of investigating structural disease.
oneLinePearl: Typical reflux is often clinical; alarm features change the pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology GERD resources

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and H. pylori: Find the Cause and Prove Eradication
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly driven by H. pylori or NSAID/aspirin exposure. Test for active H. pylori with a validated nonserologic strategy when appropriate, treat using a current resistance-aware Canadian regimen, remove ulcerogenic exposure when possible, and confirm eradication after therapy instead of assuming symptom improvement equals cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain/dyspepsia may occur, but ulcer disease can present first with bleeding, anemia, perforation or gastric outlet obstruction.
NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants and corticosteroid combinations increase bleeding risk, especially in older adults or prior ulcer disease.
differentiate: H. pylori serology may remain positive after eradication and is not the preferred test of cure.
Severe sudden abdominal pain/rigidity suggests perforation; melena/hematemesis with instability is an acute GI-bleed pathway rather than routine dyspepsia care.
assessment: Review prior H. pylori treatment, NSAID/aspirin use, anticoagulants, smoking, bleeding symptoms, anemia/weight loss, family/gastric-cancer risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use urea breath or stool antigen testing for active infection when appropriate, accounting for medications that reduce test sensitivity.
Endoscopy is indicated for bleeding/alarm/high-risk disease and allows biopsy/testing when required.
management: Use a current Canadian/local H. pylori eradication regimen based on allergy, prior macrolide/metronidazole exposure, resistance patterns and previous failures rather than defaulting to an outdated universal triple regimen.
Provide ulcer-healing acid suppression and stop/modify NSAID exposure when possible.
Confirm eradication with an appropriate active-infection test after the guideline-specified medication washout/timing interval.
medicationSafety: Bismuth/antibiotic regimens have interaction, pregnancy and adherence issues; verify the current regimen and renal/hepatic context.
If aspirin/anticoagulation is required for high thrombotic risk, coordinate resumption after bleeding with the appropriate acute-care/specialty pathway rather than stopping indefinitely.
counselling: Explain that symptom relief does not prove H. pylori eradication and emphasize completion of the multidrug regimen.
followUp: Document test of cure and reassess ongoing NSAID/aspirin gastroprotection needs.
examTrap: Calling H. pylori cured because pain resolved without performing an appropriate test of eradication.
oneLinePearl: Treat the ulcer cause, then prove H. pylori is gone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori guidance

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features Before Endoscopy, H. pylori Before Endless PPIs
bottomLine: Uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm/high-risk features is usually managed first with a noninvasive H. pylori strategy and/or empiric acid suppression rather than routine endoscopy. Progressive dysphagia, anemia/bleeding, weight loss, persistent vomiting, older/high-gastric-cancer-risk context or treatment failure changes the diagnostic threshold.
recognize: Postprandial fullness, early satiety or epigastric pain/burning define the dyspepsia symptom complex.
Functional dyspepsia is diagnosed after appropriate evaluation excludes structural disease; it is not a dismissal of symptoms.
differentiate: GERD is dominated by heartburn/regurgitation; biliary/pancreatic disease, medication effects and cardiac disease can present with upper abdominal discomfort.
Alarm symptoms do not prove cancer but increase the need for structural evaluation.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, age/risk, dysphagia, bleeding/anemia, vomiting, weight loss, family/immigration gastric-cancer risk, NSAIDs, alcohol, cannabis and prior H. pylori treatment.
workup: For younger low-risk patients without alarm features, use noninvasive H. pylori testing and/or empiric PPI strategy rather than routine endoscopy.
Use endoscopy when alarm/high-risk features, older age/risk context or persistent refractory disease justify it; avoid upper-GI series as a routine dyspepsia test.
management: Eradicate H. pylori when present and confirm cure; use a PPI trial when appropriate.
Persistent functional dyspepsia may use dietary, neuromodulator/prokinetic or psychological approaches according to phenotype and GI guidance.
medicationSafety: Avoid indefinite PPI escalation without confirming adherence/timing and reconsidering diagnosis.
NSAIDs and other ulcerogenic drugs should be reviewed early.
counselling: Explain why an immediate scope is not always safer in a low-risk patient and provide clear alarm-feature return instructions.
followUp: Reassess after H. pylori/PPI strategy and escalate investigation if symptoms persist or evolve.
examTrap: Ordering routine endoscopy in a younger low-risk patient with uncomplicated dyspepsia before H. pylori/PPI management.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia care is risk-stratified—not everyone needs a scope first.
sourceBasis: ACG/CAG Clinical Guideline: Management of Dyspepsia

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Prove Inflammation, Define Extent, Prevent Complications
bottomLine: IBD is chronic intestinal inflammation established from clinical, biochemical/endoscopic/imaging and histologic evidence—not from diarrhea alone. Distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis, assess severity/extent and complications, exclude infection during flares, and use steroid-sparing maintenance therapy through a treat-to-target GI plan.
recognize: Bloody diarrhea, urgency, abdominal pain, weight loss, perianal disease, anemia and extraintestinal joint/skin/eye/liver manifestations can occur.
Crohn disease is transmural/segmental and can involve the GI tract/perianal region; ulcerative colitis is continuous colonic mucosal disease beginning at the rectum.
differentiate: IBS does not produce objective intestinal inflammation, bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory complications.
Infectious colitis including C. difficile can mimic an IBD flare and should be evaluated when clinically appropriate before escalating immunosuppression.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight/nutrition, fever, perianal symptoms, extraintestinal disease, smoking, pregnancy, medication adherence and immunosuppression toxicity.
workup: Use CBC/CRP and fecal inflammatory markers when useful, stool infection testing during suspected flare, and colonoscopy with biopsies plus small-bowel/imaging evaluation according to suspected extent.
Avoid relying on one inflammatory marker as proof of remission or active disease.
management: Induce and maintain remission with disease/location/severity-appropriate 5-ASA, corticosteroid, immunomodulator, biologic or small-molecule therapy through current GI pathways; systemic steroids are not maintenance therapy.
Treat abscess, obstruction, toxic colitis, severe bleeding or perforation urgently with specialist/surgical care.
Address vaccination, bone health, thrombosis risk, nutrition and cancer surveillance.
medicationSafety: Before significant immunosuppression/biologics, screen infection and vaccination risks according to drug class and current guidance.
NSAIDs can worsen disease in some patients; immunosuppressive toxicity requires CBC/liver/infection monitoring specific to therapy.
counselling: Teach that symptom control and inflammatory control are related but not identical and emphasize medication adherence/monitoring.
followUp: Use treat-to-target follow-up with objective disease assessment, cancer surveillance and therapy monitoring through GI care.
examTrap: Escalating immunosuppression for presumed IBD flare without considering C. difficile or another enteric infection.
oneLinePearl: IBD treatment targets inflammation, not just diarrhea.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBD guideline library
Crohn's and Colitis Canada clinical resources

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis After Checking the Alarm Pattern
bottomLine: IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction diagnosed positively from recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation/stool change after alarm features and targeted mimics are considered. Do not turn IBS into a diagnosis of endless exclusion, but do not label bleeding, anemia, weight loss or objective inflammation as IBS.
recognize: Abdominal pain plus altered stool frequency/form, bloating and symptom fluctuation are common; subtype by predominant constipation, diarrhea or mixed pattern.
Symptoms can be severe without structural damage and are not 'all in the patient's head'.
differentiate: IBD, celiac disease, colorectal cancer, microscopic colitis, thyroid disease and medication effects are considered from age/risk/symptoms.
Nocturnal diarrhea, overt bleeding, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, fever or progressive weight loss are not typical IBS features.
assessment: Assess symptom criteria, stool pattern, diet triggers, medications, psychosocial stress without attribution bias, family history, celiac/IBD risk and alarm features.
workup: Use celiac serology in appropriate IBS patients and targeted CBC/CRP/fecal testing when the phenotype or alarm pattern warrants it.
Avoid routine colonoscopy in younger low-risk patients without alarm features; age/risk-appropriate colorectal screening remains separate from IBS diagnosis.
management: Use shared decision-making among dietary strategies, soluble fibre, antispasmodic/secretagogue/antidiarrheal options, neuromodulators and gut-directed psychological therapies by subtype and severity.
Avoid overly restrictive long-term diets without nutrition support.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics/TCAs can worsen constipation and cause older-adult adverse effects; diarrhea drugs can mask evolving inflammatory/infectious disease if red flags are ignored.
redFlags: Family history of colorectal cancer/IBD/celiac with concerning presentation
counselling: Validate IBS as a real gut-brain disorder and set functional goals rather than promising a single cure.
followUp: Reassess response and revisit diagnosis if alarm features or a major symptom-pattern change emerges.
examTrap: Ordering repeated CT/colonoscopy panels for stable typical IBS—or calling rectal bleeding and anemia 'IBS'.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive pattern diagnosis with an alarm-feature safety check.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Clinical Practice Guideline for IBS

title: Celiac Disease: Test While Gluten Is Still in the Diet
bottomLine: Celiac disease is immune-mediated gluten-related enteropathy confirmed with appropriate serology and, in most adults, small-bowel histology while the patient is consuming gluten. Do not recommend a gluten-free trial before testing when diagnosis matters, because gluten withdrawal can normalize the evidence needed to confirm disease.
recognize: Diarrhea, bloating, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, osteoporosis, infertility, elevated transaminases, dermatitis herpetiformis or no GI symptoms can occur.
Risk rises with first-degree family history, type 1 diabetes and selected autoimmune/genetic conditions.
differentiate: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity and wheat/FODMAP intolerance do not produce the same autoimmune serology/histology.
IgA deficiency can make standard IgA-based serology falsely negative and requires an alternate strategy.
assessment: Confirm current gluten intake, symptoms, family/autoimmune history, anemia/nutritional status, bone risk and prior self-directed diet restriction.
workup: Use tissue-transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA as a common first-line approach, with IgG-based testing when IgA deficient; refer for endoscopic duodenal biopsy according to adult diagnostic guidance.
If already gluten-free, do not interpret negative serology as exclusion without considering HLA/testing or supervised gluten challenge strategy.
management: Treat confirmed disease with lifelong strict gluten-free diet supported by a knowledgeable dietitian and assess iron/folate/B12/vitamin D/bone or other deficiencies as indicated.
Screen/manage associated autoimmune and bone-health issues and ensure vaccination/splenism considerations when clinically relevant.
medicationSafety: Check medication/supplement formulations when gluten exposure is plausible, but avoid creating unnecessary medication avoidance without evidence.
Do not prescribe corticosteroids for routine celiac disease; refractory disease needs specialist confirmation.
redFlags: Persistent symptoms/weight loss despite strict diet
counselling: Explain cross-contamination, label reading and why diagnosis should be established before lifelong dietary restriction.
followUp: Track symptoms, nutritional deficiencies and celiac serology trend when appropriate; persistent abnormality prompts diet/adherence and alternate-diagnosis review.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop gluten before celiac serology/biopsy and then interpreting normalized tests as proof they never had celiac disease.
oneLinePearl: If you want to diagnose celiac disease, test before the gluten disappears.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology/celiac practice resources

title: Hepatitis B and C: Define Active Infection, Stage Liver Risk, Treat the Right Virus
bottomLine: HBV and HCV require different virologic reasoning. For HBV, define infection phase with serology, HBV DNA, ALT and fibrosis/clinical context before deciding on long-term antiviral therapy. For HCV, confirm active infection with HCV RNA and link most patients to curative direct-acting antiviral therapy rather than using antibody positivity as proof of current infection.
recognize: HBsAg indicates current HBV infection; anti-HBc/anti-HBs patterns distinguish exposure/immunity and require correct interpretation.
HCV antibody shows prior exposure but cannot distinguish spontaneous/treated cure from active infection; HCV RNA confirms current viremia.
differentiate: HBV treatment may be long-term suppression and is based on viral load, ALT, fibrosis/cirrhosis and special populations; HCV treatment is generally finite curative DAA therapy.
Acute severe hepatitis, decompensated cirrhosis, pregnancy/perinatal HBV risk and immunosuppression/reactivation require different urgency.
assessment: Assess country of origin/risk, injection/sexual/blood exposure, pregnancy, HIV/coinfection, alcohol, metabolic liver risk, immunosuppression, family HCC history and signs of cirrhosis.
workup: For HBV use complete serologic/virologic staging, ALT and noninvasive fibrosis assessment; evaluate HCC surveillance eligibility.
For HCV obtain RNA confirmation, fibrosis/cirrhosis assessment and treatment-relevant renal/hepatic/drug-interaction testing; genotype requirements depend on current regimen/pathway.
management: Use the current 2025 CASL/AMMI HBV treatment algorithm and refer complex cirrhosis/pregnancy/coinfection/immune-suppression cases appropriately.
Treat active HCV with a current pan-genotypic/appropriate DAA regimen and document sustained virologic response after therapy.
Vaccinate susceptible contacts/patients for hepatitis A/B as indicated and address harm reduction.
medicationSafety: HBV can reactivate with chemotherapy/biologics or after stopping suppressive therapy; screen before high-risk immunosuppression and use prophylaxis/monitoring as indicated.
DAAs have clinically important interactions and decompensated cirrhosis changes regimen eligibility; verify the current Canadian pathway.
redFlags: Pregnancy with high HBV transmission risk
counselling: Explain that HCV antibody can remain positive after cure and that HBV suppression is not the same as eradication.
Use non-stigmatizing harm-reduction and partner/household prevention counselling.
followUp: Document HCV cure; continue cirrhosis/HCC surveillance when indicated despite cure. For HBV, track DNA/ALT/fibrosis/HCC risk according to treatment status and guideline.
examTrap: Calling a positive HCV antibody 'active hepatitis C' without ordering HCV RNA—or treating HBV from HBsAg alone without phase/fibrosis context.
oneLinePearl: HBV is phase-and-fibrosis driven; HCV antibody needs RNA to prove active infection.
